unit_label: Introduction to Number System and Logic Gates

questions.q: What is the base (radix) of the octal number system?
questions.explain: Octal uses digits 0 to 7, so its radix is 8.
why_wrong: Base 2 is binary.
Base 10 is decimal.
Base 16 is hexadecimal.

questions.q: Which hexadecimal symbol represents the decimal value 12?
questions.explain: Hex digits A to F stand for 10 to 15 in order, so 12 is C.
why_wrong: A stands for decimal 10.
B stands for decimal 11.
D stands for decimal 13.

questions.q: What is the binary equivalent of decimal 13?
questions.explain: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, giving bits 1101.
why_wrong: 1011 is decimal 11.
1110 is decimal 14.
1001 is decimal 9.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of the binary number 1010?
why_wrong: 12 is binary 1100.
5 is binary 0101, the reversed bit order.
8 is binary 1000; the 2s place was ignored.

questions.q: How many binary bits correspond to one octal digit?
questions.explain: Octal digits go from 0 to 7, which need exactly 3 bits (2^3 = 8).
why_wrong: Two bits only reach 0 to 3, not 0 to 7.
Four bits correspond to one hexadecimal digit.
Eight bits make a byte, not an octal digit.

questions.q: In the Gray code, consecutive code words differ in how many bit positions?
questions.explain: Gray code is a unit-distance code, so each step changes a single bit.
why_wrong: Two-bit changes occur in ordinary binary counting, not in Gray code.
Four changes would be the complement of the word, not a successive step.
The Gray code guarantees a fixed single-bit change.

questions.q: Gray code is an example of which type of code?
questions.explain: Because adjacent words differ in one bit, Gray code is a unit-distance, non-weighted code.
why_wrong: Gray code bit positions have no fixed weights.
Alphanumeric codes such as ASCII represent characters.
Gray code can not correct errors; it only limits bit changes.

questions.q: When converting binary to Gray code, the MSB of the Gray code is
options: The complement of the binary MSB
XOR of the two highest binary bits
questions.explain: The first Gray bit is copied directly from the binary MSB.
why_wrong: The MSB is copied, not inverted.
That rule gives the second Gray bit.
The MSB follows the binary MSB and can be 1.

questions.q: What is the Gray code of the 2-bit binary number 10?
questions.explain: G1 = B1 = 1 and G0 = B1 XOR B0 = 1 XOR 0 = 1, giving 11.
why_wrong: The bits are unchanged, but the second bit is 1 XOR 0 = 1.
The MSB must be copied as 1, not inverted.
The MSB must be copied as 1, so the result cannot be 00.

questions.q: Excess-3 code of a decimal digit is obtained by adding what to its BCD code?
questions.explain: Excess-3 means the 8421 BCD value plus 3.
why_wrong: The excess is 3, not 2.
6 is the BCD addition correction, not the excess.
9 is the complement base, not the excess.

questions.q: Excess-3 is classified as which kind of code?
questions.explain: The 1's complement of an excess-3 word gives the code of the 9's complement digit.
why_wrong: That is the Gray code.
Excess-3 has no correction ability.
Excess-3 is an unweighted code.

questions.q: What is the excess-3 code of decimal 0?
why_wrong: That is BCD for 0.
That is excess-3 of 2.
That is excess-3 of 9.

questions.q: What is the excess-3 code of decimal 5?
why_wrong: That is plain BCD for 5.
That is excess-3 of 0.
That is excess-3 of 9.

questions.q: What is the BCD code of decimal 9?
questions.explain: BCD encodes each digit by its 4-bit binary value, and 9 = 1001.
why_wrong: 0111 is BCD for 7.
1000 is BCD for 8.
1111 is not a valid BCD digit.

questions.q: How many bits does BCD use to encode one decimal digit?
questions.explain: Digits 0 to 9 need four bits, so BCD uses 4 bits per digit.
why_wrong: Three bits only reach 7.
Eight bits is packed or ASCII style storage.
Ten is the number of digits, not bits.

questions.q: What are the bit weights in 8421 BCD, from MSB to LSB?
questions.explain: The name 8421 gives the weights directly.
why_wrong: The weights are powers of two, not consecutive integers.
These are not the BCD weights.
These are not the BCD weights.

questions.q: Which 4-bit pattern is NOT a valid BCD digit?
questions.explain: BCD only uses 0000 to 1001, so 1010 to 1111 are invalid.
why_wrong: This is BCD for 9.
This is BCD for 7.
This is BCD for 0.

questions.q: What is the 1's complement of the binary number 1010?
questions.explain: The 1's complement flips every bit, so 1010 becomes 0101.
why_wrong: This inverts only some bits, which is not the 1's complement.
This is the original number.
This is the number plus 1.

questions.q: How is the 2's complement of a binary number obtained?
options: Reverse the order of its bits
questions.explain: 2's complement = 1's complement + 1.
why_wrong: This is the wrong direction.
Reversal is not complementing.
That is just incrementing, not complementing.

questions.q: What is the 1's complement of the 4-bit number 0000?
questions.explain: Flipping all four bits gives 1111.
why_wrong: The bits must all be flipped.
This is the 2's complement attempt without flipping.
Only the MSB was flipped.

questions.q: In a signed 2's complement number, an MSB of 1 indicates that the number is
questions.explain: The MSB is the sign bit and 1 means negative.
why_wrong: A positive number has MSB 0.
Zero is all 0 bits.
Overflow is a result condition, not a property of the MSB.

questions.q: What is the range of a 4-bit signed 2's complement number?
questions.explain: n-bit 2's complement spans -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1, i.e. -8 to +7.
why_wrong: That is the 1's complement and sign-magnitude range.
+8 needs 5 bits.
That is the unsigned range.

questions.q: What is the binary sum 1 + 1?
questions.explain: 1 + 1 gives sum 0 and carry 1, which reads 10.
why_wrong: The carry is lost; the sum is 0 with carry 1.
2 is not a binary digit.

questions.q: What is the binary sum 1 + 1 + 1?
questions.explain: Three ones sum to 3, which is 11 in binary.
why_wrong: That is only two ones.
That ignores the carry.
That is not an addition result.

questions.q: To compute A - B using 2's complement, we add A to what?
questions.explain: A - B = A + (2's complement of B).
why_wrong: The subtrahend is complemented, not the minuend.
That would compute A + B.
The subtrahend B is complemented, not A.

questions.q: In 2's complement subtraction, an end carry out of the MSB tells us the result is
questions.explain: With an end carry, the result is positive and the carry is dropped.
why_wrong: A negative result gives no end carry.
Zero is not the only case.
The end carry is normal in valid subtraction.

questions.q: A 2-input AND gate gives output 1 only when
questions.explain: AND is the product operation, so it is high only for all inputs high.
why_wrong: That describes OR.
That describes XOR.
That describes NOR.

questions.q: Which logic gate performs the inversion (complement) of a single input?
questions.explain: The NOT gate (inverter) outputs the complement of its input.
why_wrong: AND combines two or more inputs.
OR combines two or more inputs.
XOR compares two inputs.

questions.q: Which two gates are called universal gates?
questions.explain: NAND and NOR can each realise any Boolean function.
why_wrong: These cannot produce inversion alone.
These cannot build every function alone.
This pair is not universal individually as a single gate.

questions.q: A 2-input XOR gate outputs 1 when its inputs are
questions.explain: XOR is the inequality gate: high when inputs differ.
why_wrong: XOR gives 0 here.
XOR gives 0 here.
That describes XNOR.

questions.q: A 2-input OR gate outputs 0 only when
questions.explain: OR gives 1 if any input is 1, so 0 only when all are 0.
why_wrong: OR outputs 1 here.
OR outputs 1 here.
OR outputs 1 here.

questions.q: In Boolean algebra, A + 0 equals
questions.explain: 0 is the identity for OR, so A + 0 = A.
why_wrong: 0 would be A.0.
1 would be A + 1.
Complement is not involved.

questions.q: In Boolean algebra, A . A' equals
questions.explain: A variable and its complement can never both be 1, so the AND is 0.
why_wrong: A + A' equals 1.
A.A equals A.
Not an identity here.

questions.q: According to De Morgan's theorem, NOT(A.B) equals
questions.explain: De Morgan: complement of a product is the sum of the complements.
why_wrong: That is NOT(A+B).
No complement applied.
No complement applied.

questions.q: In Boolean algebra, A + 1 equals
questions.explain: OR with 1 always gives 1.
why_wrong: That is A.1.
That is A.0.
Not an identity.

questions.q: The double complement NOT(NOT A) equals
questions.explain: Inverting twice restores the original value.
why_wrong: A single complement gives this.
Not valid.
Not valid.

questions.q: A Sum-of-Products (SOP) expression is
options: A single XOR of all variables
questions.explain: SOP ORs together product (AND) terms.
why_wrong: That is POS.
That is parity form.
That is not the definition.

questions.q: The minterm m0 of three variables A, B, C is
questions.explain: m0 corresponds to 000, so every variable is complemented in a product.
why_wrong: That is the maxterm M0.
That is minterm m7.
That is the maxterm M7.

questions.q: When writing SOP from a truth table, we pick the rows where the output is
questions.explain: Each output-1 row gives one minterm that is ORed into the SOP.
why_wrong: Those rows give the POS form.
Don't cares are optional, not defined.
No such rule exists.

questions.q: A Product-of-Sums (POS) expression is
questions.explain: POS ANDs together sum (OR) terms.
why_wrong: That is SOP.
Not the definition.
Not the definition.

questions.q: How many cells does a 3-variable K-map have?
questions.explain: A K-map has 2^n cells, so 2^3 = 8.
why_wrong: 4 cells is a 2-variable map.
Not a power of 2.
16 cells is a 4-variable map.

questions.q: How many cells does a 4-variable K-map have?
questions.explain: 2^4 = 16 cells.
why_wrong: 8 cells is a 3-variable map.
4 cells is a 2-variable map.
32 cells is a 5-variable map.

questions.q: Along the sides of a K-map, the row/column labels are arranged in which order?
questions.explain: Labels follow 00, 01, 11, 10 so adjacent cells differ in one variable.
why_wrong: Binary order would put two bit changes between neighbours.
The order is fixed.
Not used.

questions.q: Groups of adjacent 1s in a K-map must contain how many cells?
questions.explain: Valid groups are 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells.
why_wrong: Only power of 2 groups are valid.
Odd groups can not be simplified.
Not a valid grouping size.

questions.q: Cells in the leftmost and rightmost columns of a K-map are
questions.explain: The edges wrap, so groups can cross them.
why_wrong: The map wraps around.
Cell values are independent of position.
Position does not decide don't care.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of the hexadecimal number 2F?
why_wrong: This treats the 2 as 2x10 + 15.
This forgets to add F (15).
This multiplies 2 by 15 instead of 16.

questions.q: Convert binary 110101 to octal.
questions.explain: Group in threes: 110 = 6, 101 = 5, so 65.
why_wrong: This is the decimal value of the number.
The two groups were swapped.
The group 101 was misread as 7.

questions.q: What is decimal 0.625 in binary?
why_wrong: This equals 0.75.
This equals 0.375.
This equals 0.5.

questions.q: Convert hexadecimal B7 to binary.
why_wrong: The second nibble should be 7 = 0111.
The nibbles are swapped.

questions.q: Convert decimal 45 to hexadecimal.
why_wrong: 2B equals 43.
The digits are reversed (210).
2E equals 46.

questions.q: What is the Gray code of binary 1011?
why_wrong: The XORs were skipped for the last bit.
This is not the XOR chain.
The MSB was complemented.

questions.q: What is the binary equivalent of the Gray code 1101?
why_wrong: The Gray bits were copied without converting.
The XOR chain was wrongly applied.
The chain was wrongly started.

questions.q: What is the 4-bit Gray code of decimal 7?
why_wrong: This is the plain binary of 7.
This is the Gray code of 4.
This is the Gray code of 15.

questions.q: How many bit positions differ between the Gray codes of decimal 7 and decimal 8?
questions.explain: Gray(7) = 0100 and Gray(8) = 1100, which differ in only the MSB.
why_wrong: That is how many binary bits change, 0111 to 1000.
Two would break the unit-distance rule.
Three would break the unit-distance rule.

questions.q: What is the excess-3 code of decimal 47?
why_wrong: This is plain BCD.
Only the first digit had 3 added.
The digit codes are swapped.

questions.q: What decimal number does the excess-3 code 1001 0110 represent?
why_wrong: This reads the code as plain BCD.
3 was subtracted only from the first group.
3 was subtracted only from the second group.

questions.q: Which of these 4-bit patterns is NOT a valid excess-3 code word?
questions.explain: Valid excess-3 words span 0011 to 1100, so 0010 is invalid.
why_wrong: This is excess-3 of 0.
This is excess-3 of 4.
This is excess-3 of 9.

questions.q: Taking the 1's complement of the excess-3 code of decimal 6 gives the excess-3 code of which digit?
questions.explain: 6 is 1001, whose complement 0110 is excess-3 of 3, the 9's complement of 6.
why_wrong: This is not the 9's complement of 6.
This reads the complemented word as BCD.
9 is the complement base, not the result.

questions.q: What is the BCD representation of decimal 259?
questions.explain: Encode digits 2, 5, 9 as 0010, 0101, 1001.
why_wrong: This is a binary conversion.
This is the excess-3 code of 259, not its plain BCD.
9 was coded wrongly as 1000.

questions.q: What decimal number is represented by the BCD 0111 0100 0011?
why_wrong: This reads the nibbles as hexadecimal.
This sums the digits.
The digits are reversed.

questions.q: How many bits are needed to store a 4-digit decimal number in BCD?
questions.explain: 4 digits x 4 bits each = 16 bits.
why_wrong: 14 is the pure binary requirement for 9999.
Only three digits would fit.
Only two digits would fit.

questions.q: In BCD addition, a digit sum greater than 9 is corrected by adding
questions.explain: Six invalid states skip, so adding 6 (0110) restores BCD.
why_wrong: This is the excess-3 offset.
This is 9, which is wrong.
This is 10, which is wrong.

questions.q: What is the 2's complement of the 5-bit number 01101?
questions.explain: 1's complement = 10010; adding 1 gives 10011.
why_wrong: This is the 1's complement without adding 1.
This is the 2's complement of 01100.
This is the original number.

questions.q: What is the 8-bit 2's complement representation of -5?
why_wrong: This is the 1's complement; no 1 was added.
This is the sign-magnitude form.
This is +5.

questions.q: What decimal value does the 4-bit 2's complement number 1011 represent?
questions.explain: Invert to 0100, add 1 to get 0101 = 5, so the value is -5.
why_wrong: This reads sign-magnitude.
This reads the 1's complement.
This reads unsigned.

questions.q: Using the copy-up-to-first-1 shortcut, the 2's complement of 10100 is
questions.explain: Copy 100, invert the leftmost two bits (10 becomes 01) to get 01100.
why_wrong: This is the 1's complement; no 1 was added.
This is the original number.
This added 2 instead of 1.

questions.q: What is the smallest number of bits that can hold -20 in 2's complement?
questions.explain: 5 bits span -16 to +15 and 6 bits span -32 to +31, so 6 are needed.
why_wrong: 5 bits only reach -16.
7 bits is more than needed.
8 bits is more than needed.

questions.q: What is 1011 + 0110 in binary?
why_wrong: This equals 16.
The carry out was dropped.
This equals 21.

questions.q: What is 10110 + 1011 in binary?
why_wrong: This equals 35.
The end carry was dropped.
This equals 32.

questions.q: Compute 1101 - 0101 using 2's complement addition (discard the end carry).
questions.explain: 2's complement of 0101 is 1011; 1101 + 1011 = 11000, drop carry to get 1000 = 8.
why_wrong: The 1's complement was used without +1.
The end carry was not discarded.
The numbers were added: 13 + 5 = 18.

questions.q: Compute 0101 - 1001 in 4-bit 2's complement; what is the result?
questions.explain: 2's complement of 1001 is 0111; 0101 + 0111 = 1100 (no carry) so it is -4.
why_wrong: The negative sign was ignored.
The 1's complement was used without +1.
Only the 2's complement of the subtrahend was taken.

questions.q: Adding 0111 and 0101 in 4-bit 2's complement gives 1100. This indicates
questions.explain: 7 + 5 = 12 exceeds +7, so the sign flipped due to overflow.
why_wrong: 7 + 5 = 12, not -4; the pattern 1100 is just 12 wrapped around in 4 bits.
Underflow is for negative operands.
No carry out of the MSB occurred.

questions.q: The XNOR gate is also known as the
questions.explain: XNOR outputs 1 when inputs are equal.
why_wrong: That describes XOR.
XNOR is not universal.
A buffer has one input.

questions.q: A 3-input XOR gate outputs 1 when
options: An odd number of inputs are 1
An even number of inputs are 1
questions.explain: XOR extends to parity: output 1 for an odd number of ones.
why_wrong: Odd count also includes 1 or 3 ones.
This is the XNOR behaviour.
This is OR behaviour.

questions.q: Both inputs of a 2-input NAND gate are connected to A. The output is
questions.explain: NAND(A,A) = (A.A)' = A'.
why_wrong: This would be a buffer.
This is a constant.
This is a constant.

questions.q: If one input of a 2-input OR gate is held at 1, the output is
options: The complement of the other input
questions.explain: A + 1 = 1 whatever the other input is.
why_wrong: That would be if the fixed input was 0.
OR does not invert.
OR with 1 is never 0.

questions.q: How many rows does the truth table of a 4-input gate have?
questions.explain: n inputs give 2^n = 16 combinations for n = 4.
why_wrong: That is 2^2.
That is 2^3.
That is 2^5.

questions.q: The identity A + B.C = (A + B).(A + C) is known as the
questions.explain: OR distributes over AND just as AND distributes over OR.
why_wrong: Absorption is A + A.B = A.
Associative law only regroups the same operation.
Commutative law only swaps operand order.

questions.q: Simplify A + A'.B.
questions.explain: A + A'B = (A + A')(A + B) = A + B.
why_wrong: B was lost.
A was lost.
Wrong operation.

questions.q: Simplify A.(A + B).
questions.explain: A.A + A.B = A + A.B = A.
why_wrong: This confuses it with a different law.
Wrong operation.
A was lost.

questions.q: The dual of the expression A + B.C is
questions.explain: The dual swaps + and . without complementing variables.
why_wrong: The variables were also complemented.
Only the AND was swapped.
The variables were complemented without swapping.

questions.q: Simplify A.B + A.B' + A'.B.
questions.explain: A.B + A.B' = A, then A + A'.B = A + B.
why_wrong: Terms were lost.
Wrong complement.
XOR omits the A.B case.

questions.q: For variables A, B, C (A is MSB), the minterm m5 is
questions.explain: 5 = 101, so A is true, B complemented, C true.
why_wrong: This is m2 (010).
This is the maxterm M5.
This is m6 (110).

questions.q: For variables A, B, C (A is MSB), the maxterm M3 is
questions.explain: 3 = 011; maxterms use the complement for each 1 bit, giving A + B' + C'.
why_wrong: This is M4.
This is minterm m3.
This is M1.

questions.q: F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,2,7). Its POS form is
questions.explain: The maxterms come from the minterm indices that are absent.
why_wrong: The same indices were reused.
Only odd numbers were taken.
Index 1 was missed.

questions.q: A 3-variable function has 3 minterms in its SOP. How many maxterms are in its POS?
questions.explain: Total 8 - 3 = 5.
why_wrong: Equal to the SOP count by mistake.
This is the total number of cells.
Not a valid count.

questions.q: Simplify F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,1,2,3) with A as MSB.
questions.explain: Minterms 0 to 3 all have A = 0 with B and C taking all values, leaving A'.
why_wrong: The wrong variable was eliminated.
The wrong variable was eliminated.
The function is not constant.

questions.q: Simplify F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,2,8,10).
why_wrong: The wrong variables were kept.
The variables are not complemented.
The wrong variables were kept.

questions.q: A group of 8 adjacent 1s in a 4-variable K-map gives a product term of how many literals?
questions.explain: Octet eliminates 3 variables, leaving 1 literal.
why_wrong: Octets eliminate 3 variables, not 2.
Octets eliminate 3 variables, leaving only 1.
No variable would be eliminated.

questions.q: Simplify F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(5,7,13,15).
why_wrong: The wrong variable was kept.
The wrong variable was kept.
One literal was complemented.

questions.q: A student reads the hex value 3A7.C from a debugger and needs its decimal value. What is it?
why_wrong: Treats the fractional hex digit C as the decimal digits 12 instead of 12/16 = 0.75.
Uses 9 for the hex digit A (A = 10), giving 3x256 + 9x16 + 7 = 919.
Reverses the weights of the integer digits (3x1 + 10x16 + 7x256).

questions.q: A firmware log prints a register as octal 7345, but the datasheet lists values in hex. What is the hex value?
questions.explain: Octal 7345 = 111 011 100 101 in binary. Regroup in fours: 1110 1110 0101 = E E 5, so the hex value is EE5.
why_wrong: Reads 7345 as a decimal number and converts that to hex.
Stops at the decimal value (7345 octal = 3813) and forgets to convert it into hex.
Writes the octal digit 3 as 100 instead of 011 when expanding to binary.

questions.q: A DAC needs the fraction 0.6875 as a binary fraction. Which bit pattern is correct?
why_wrong: Reads the bits in reverse order (0.1101 = 0.8125).
Equals 0.5625; the 1/4 place was skipped during repeated doubling.
Equals 0.875; the last doubling step was misread.

questions.q: A technician sees the hex value 0x26B in a microcontroller register and needs the decimal value. Which is it?
why_wrong: Takes the hex digit B as 12 instead of 11.
Takes the hex digit B as 10 instead of 11.
Simply adds the digit values 2 + 6 + 11 without using powers of 16.

questions.q: A 10-bit ADC outputs 1101101101. The panel meter shows readings in octal. What does it display?
questions.explain: Group from the right in threes: 1 | 101 | 101 | 101 = 1 5 5 5. So the octal reading is 1555 (decimal 877).
why_wrong: Groups the bits in threes from the left (110 110 110 1) and pads the last group on the right as 100, giving 6664.
Gives the decimal value instead of the octal representation.
Writes one group (101) as 011 while converting the middle digit.

questions.q: In which number base does the product 3 x 4 equal 10?
questions.explain: 3 x 4 = 12 in decimal. The numeral 10 in base b means b, so b = 12.
why_wrong: Confuses the sum 3 + 4 = 7 with the product.
In base 10 the product 3 x 4 is written 12, not 10.
In base 16 the product 12 is written C, not 10.

questions.q: Convert the hex number FF.8 into octal.
questions.explain: FF.8 = 1111 1111 . 1000 in binary. Regroup in threes: 011 111 111 . 100 = 377.4 (decimal 255.5).
why_wrong: 8 is not a legal octal digit; the hex fraction digit was copied across.
Equals 377.25; the fraction .5 was mapped to digit 2 instead of 4.
Reverses the order of the integer digits.

questions.q: If (121) in some base x equals decimal 36, what is x?
why_wrong: Takes the square root of 36; but 121 in base 6 is 36 + 12 + 1 = 49.
Gives 121 in base 7 = 49 + 14 + 1 = 64, not 36.
Gives 121 in base 4 = 16 + 8 + 1 = 25, not 36.

questions.q: An encoder designer must convert the binary word 1011 to Gray code. Which is the Gray word?
questions.explain: The Gray MSB equals the binary MSB (1). Each next bit is the XOR of adjacent binary bits: 1^0 = 1, 0^1 = 1, 1^1 = 0. So the Gray word is 1110.
why_wrong: Applies the XOR between each bit and the bit on its right instead of its left neighbour.
Uses XNOR instead of XOR between adjacent bits.
Uses OR instead of XOR between adjacent bits.

questions.q: A rotary encoder outputs the Gray word 1101. What is the equivalent binary count?
questions.explain: Binary MSB = Gray MSB = 1. Each next binary bit = previous binary bit XOR current Gray bit: 1^1 = 0, 0^0 = 0, 0^1 = 1. So the binary word is 1001 (decimal 9).
why_wrong: Applies the binary-to-Gray rule to 1101 instead of the Gray-to-binary rule.
Uses OR instead of XOR when chaining the bits.
Uses XNOR instead of XOR when chaining the bits.

questions.q: A 4-bit Gray-code position sensor currently shows 0111. The shaft moves exactly one step forward in the counting direction. What does the sensor show next?
questions.explain: 0111 is the Gray code of 5 and the next count 6 has Gray code 6 XOR 3 = 0101. Only one bit changes (the second bit), as required.
why_wrong: Adds 1 in ordinary binary (0111 + 1), which is not how Gray code counts.
This is the previous code in the sequence, one step backward.
This is the code two steps forward, not one.

questions.q: A shaft encoder moves from position 7 to position 8. How many output bits change in a 4-bit binary encoder and in a 4-bit Gray encoder?
questions.explain: Binary 0111 to 1000 flips all four bits. Gray 0100 to 1100 flips only the MSB. This single-bit change is why Gray code is used to avoid glitches in encoders.
why_wrong: Swaps the two cases.
Counts only the three bits that fall to 0 and forgets that the new MSB also changes.
Assumes two Gray bits change; Gray code always changes exactly one bit per step.

questions.q: A counter's 8-bit binary value is decimal 100 (01100100). What Gray word should be sent to the Gray-coded display driver?
questions.explain: Gray = B XOR (B >> 1) = 01100100 XOR 00110010 = 01010110. The MSB stays 0 and each other bit is the XOR of two adjacent binary bits.
why_wrong: Uses OR instead of XOR between adjacent bits.
Uses XNOR instead of XOR between adjacent bits.
XORs with the left-shifted word instead of the right-shifted word.

questions.q: How many bit positions differ between the 4-bit Gray codes of decimal 15 and decimal 0?
questions.explain: Gray(15) = 1000 and Gray(0) = 0000, so only the MSB differs. Gray code is cyclic: the last code differs from the first in one bit.
why_wrong: This is the difference between their binary codes 1111 and 0000.
Gray code never changes two bits between neighbouring counts, and 15 to 0 is a neighbouring pair.
Counts the bits that differ in 1111 versus 0001; not a valid comparison.

questions.q: A 4-bit Gray word 1010 is received. What is the corresponding decimal count?
questions.explain: Gray-to-binary: b3 = 1, b2 = 1^0 = 1, b1 = 1^1 = 0, b0 = 0^0 = 0, so the binary word is 1100 = 12.
why_wrong: Reads the Gray word directly as an ordinary binary number.
Applies the binary-to-Gray rule to 1010 (giving 1111) instead of Gray-to-binary.
Uses XNOR instead of XOR in the Gray-to-binary chain (giving 1001).

questions.q: Which of these 4-bit Gray words belongs to an odd decimal count?
questions.explain: Each Gray step flips exactly one bit, so the number of 1s alternates between even and odd. Count 0 has weight 0, so odd counts have odd weight: only 1101 (Gray code of 9) has an odd number of 1s.
why_wrong: This is the Gray code of the even count 4.
This is the Gray code of the even count 8.
This is the Gray code of the even count 12.

questions.q: A display driver needs the excess-3 code for decimal 47. Which code should be sent?
questions.explain: Excess-3 adds 3 to each decimal digit separately: 4+3 = 7 = 0111 and 7+3 = 10 = 1010. So 47 is 0111 1010.
why_wrong: This is plain BCD of 47; the 3 was never added to each digit.
Adds 3 to the whole number first (47 + 3 = 50) and then encodes it in BCD.
Adds 3 only to the first digit and leaves the second digit as plain BCD.

questions.q: A BCD adder adds the digits 6 (0110) and 7 (0111). What is the correctly adjusted BCD result?
questions.explain: 0110 + 0111 = 1101 (13), which is above 9, so add the correction 0110: 1101 + 0110 = 1 0011. The BCD result is 0001 0011 = 13.
why_wrong: The raw binary sum, which is an invalid BCD digit and has not been corrected.
Adds the correction 0011 instead of 0110.
Adds 0111 instead of 0110 as the correction.

questions.q: A meter sends two excess-3 digits 1000 0101. What decimal reading does it represent?
questions.explain: Subtract 3 from each nibble: 1000 - 0011 = 0101 = 5 and 0101 - 0011 = 0010 = 2. So the reading is 52.
why_wrong: Reads the nibbles as plain BCD without subtracting 3.
Reads the 8 bits as one ordinary binary number (10000101 = 133).
Subtracts 3 from the second digit only.

questions.q: In an excess-3 decimal system, decimal digit 2 is stored as 0101. Without any arithmetic, which excess-3 word represents its 9's complement digit?
questions.explain: Excess-3 is self-complementing: inverting every bit gives the code of the 9's complement digit. 9 - 2 = 7, and the inverse of 0101 is 1010, which is excess-3 of 7.
why_wrong: This is plain BCD of 7, the 9's complement digit, not its excess-3 code.
This is the excess-3 code of 6, not 7.
This is the excess-3 code of 8, not 7.

questions.q: Add the BCD numbers 0111 1001 (79) and 0011 0101 (35). What is the correct BCD result?
why_wrong: Forgets to add the carry from the corrected low digit into the high digit.
Corrects the low digit but never corrects the invalid high digit 1011.
The raw 8-bit binary sum with no BCD correction at all.

questions.q: Two excess-3 digits 0101 (decimal 2) and 0110 (decimal 3) are added. What is the correct excess-3 sum digit?
questions.explain: 0101 + 0110 = 1011 with no carry out. In excess-3 addition, subtract 0011 when there is no carry: 1011 - 0011 = 1000, which is excess-3 of 5.
why_wrong: The raw binary sum, left uncorrected.
Adds 0011 as if there were a carry, instead of subtracting it.
This is plain BCD of 5, not the excess-3 code.

questions.q: Decimal 2025 is stored in BCD and, separately, as a plain binary number. How many more bits does the BCD form use?
questions.explain: BCD uses 4 bits per digit, so 4 digits need 16 bits. Plain binary needs 11 bits because 1024 <= 2025 < 2048. The difference is 16 - 11 = 5.
why_wrong: Assumes the binary form needs 12 bits.
Assumes the binary form needs only 10 bits, but 2025 is above 1023.
Counts only the BCD bits and ignores the binary form.

questions.q: A DSP stores -108 by negating the 8-bit value 01101100. What is the 2's complement pattern?
questions.explain: Invert 01101100 to get 10010011, then add 1 to get 10010100. Check: 01101100 + 10010100 = 1 00000000, so the sum is 0 in 8 bits.
why_wrong: This is only the 1's complement; the +1 step was skipped.
Adds 1 to the original number without inverting it first.
Adds the 1 in the second bit position instead of the least significant bit.

questions.q: An 8-bit register in 2's complement holds 11010110. What signed value does it represent?
questions.explain: The sign bit is 1, so the number is negative. Invert 11010110 to 00101001 and add 1 to get 00101010 = 42, so the value is -42 (equivalently 214 - 256).
why_wrong: Reads the pattern as an unsigned binary number.
Uses the 1's complement interpretation (invert only, no +1).
Uses a sign-magnitude interpretation (sign bit 1, magnitude 1010110).

questions.q: A sensor reports temperatures between -100 and +90 (whole units). What is the minimum number of bits needed to store every reading in 2's complement?
questions.explain: An n-bit 2's complement number covers -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1. For 7 bits that is -64..63 (too small); for 8 bits it is -128..127, which covers -100..+90.
why_wrong: A 7-bit 2's complement field only covers -64 to +63.
Works, but 8 bits already cover -128 to +127, so 9 is not the minimum.
A 6-bit field only covers -32 to +31.

questions.q: A hex byte 0xB4 is a signed 8-bit 2's complement value. A routine negates it by taking the 2's complement. What hex byte results?
questions.explain: B4 = 1011 0100. Invert to 0100 1011 (4B) and add 1 to get 0100 1100 = 4C. Check: B4 + 4C = 100 hex, which is 0 in 8 bits.
why_wrong: This is the 1's complement of B4; the +1 step was skipped.
Adds 1 after the inversion and then adds one more.
Swaps nibbles of the hex digits, which is unrelated to complementing.

questions.q: In a 4-bit 2's complement system, the 2's complement of 1000 (which is -8) is taken. What is the result?
questions.explain: Invert 1000 to 0111, add 1 to get 1000. +8 cannot be represented in 4 bits (max +7), so the most negative number is its own negation and the operation overflows.
why_wrong: This is the 1's complement; adding 1 gives 1000 again.
Assumes -(-8) must wrap to zero, which it does not.
Adds 1 to 1000 without inverting first.

questions.q: In an 8-bit system, the pattern 11111111 is interpreted first in 1's complement and then in 2's complement. What values result?
questions.explain: In 1's complement, all-ones is the inverse of all-zeros, i.e. -0. In 2's complement, invert to 00000000 and add 1 to get 1, so the value is -1.
why_wrong: Swaps the two interpretations.
Takes sign-magnitude for the first interpretation (1 then 1111111).
Gives the right 1's complement reading but uses sign-magnitude for the second.

questions.q: The 4-bit 2's complement number 1010 is stored into an 8-bit register by sign extension. What 8-bit pattern results?
questions.explain: 4-bit 1010 = 10 - 16 = -6. Sign extension copies the sign bit into the new high bits to preserve the value: 1111 1010, which is -128+64+32+16+8+2 = -6.
why_wrong: Zero-extends the word, changing the value from -6 to +10.
Sign-magnitude style extension, which reads as -10.
This is the 1's complement of 00001010 and represents -11.

questions.q: For 5-bit numbers, what is the most negative value that can be represented in 1's complement and in 2's complement respectively?
questions.explain: 1's complement has two zeros, so its range is -(2^4 - 1) to +(2^4 - 1) = -15..+15. 2's complement has a single zero, so its range is -16..+15.
why_wrong: Assumes 1's complement also has an extra negative value; it does not.
Assumes 2's complement loses its extra negative value.
Swaps the two systems.

questions.q: An 8-bit ALU subtracts 42 from 25 using 2's complement addition. What is the 8-bit result?
questions.explain: 25 = 00011001 and 2's complement of 42 (00101010) is 11010110. Their sum is 11101111 with no carry out, so the result is negative: invert and add 1 gives 17, i.e. -17.
why_wrong: Adds the 1's complement of 42 and forgets the final +1.
Shows the magnitude +17 instead of the signed result -17.
Writes -17 in sign-magnitude instead of 2's complement.

questions.q: Two signed 8-bit 2's complement numbers, +105 and +78, are added. How is the 8-bit result 10110111 read?
questions.explain: 105 + 78 = 183, which is above +127, so the 8-bit sum is 183 - 256 = -73 (10110111). Two positive operands gave a negative result, which signals overflow.
why_wrong: Treats the result as unsigned, ignoring that the sign bit is part of the number.
Reads it in 1's complement (invert only, no +1).
Reads it in sign-magnitude form (sign bit 1, magnitude 0110111).

questions.q: A 4-bit calculator evaluates 1101 - 0111 using 2's complement addition. What is the 4-bit result?
questions.explain: 2's complement of 0111 is 1001. Then 1101 + 1001 = 1 0110; drop the carry to get 0110 = 6, matching 13 - 7.
why_wrong: Adds the 1's complement of 0111 and forgets the +1.
Adds 0111 instead of subtracting it.
Adds only the 2's complement of the subtrahend and forgets to add 1101.

questions.q: A 4-bit unsigned accumulator holds 1011 (11). The program adds 1101 (13) twice, and any carry out is discarded. What does the accumulator hold at the end?
why_wrong: This is the value after only the first addition (24 mod 16 = 8).
Ignores the additions and shows only the operand.
Keeps the carried bits as if the register were 5 bits wide.

questions.q: In 4-bit 2's complement arithmetic, which addition produces a signed overflow?
questions.explain: 0110 + 0011 is 6 + 3 = 9, which exceeds +7, giving 1001 (-7): two positives yield a negative result, so overflow. A carry out alone does not mean signed overflow.
why_wrong: (-4) + (-3) = -7 fits; the carry out is 1 but no signed overflow occurs.
5 + 2 = 7 fits within the range -8 to +7.
(-5) + 4 = -1; operands of different signs can never overflow.

questions.q: A 4-bit unsigned subtraction 0101 - 1001 is done by adding the 2's complement of 1001. What are the 4-bit result and the carry out?
questions.explain: 2's complement of 1001 is 0111. 0101 + 0111 = 01100: 4-bit result 1100 and carry out 0. For subtraction a carry out of 0 signals a borrow, i.e. the answer is negative (1100 = -4).
why_wrong: Carry out 1 would mean no borrow, which only happens when the minuend is the larger value.
Writes the magnitude 4 instead of the actual 4-bit result -4 = 1100.
Writes the magnitude and also claims no borrow.

questions.q: A 4-bit adder adds 1111 and 1111, producing 1110 with carry out 1. Which statement is correct?
options: Signed overflow occurred, because the carry out is 1 here
The result is 1111 and no carry is produced
Signed -1 + -1 = -2 is valid; carry is unsigned only
As signed numbers the result is +14, which is valid
questions.explain: 1111 + 1111 = 1 1110. In 2's complement 1111 = -1, so the sum is -2 (1110), a valid result with no signed overflow. In unsigned terms 15 + 15 = 30 does not fit, so the carry flags unsigned overflow.
why_wrong: Signed overflow depends on the sign bits, not on the carry out.
Misstates the sum; 15 + 15 = 30 = 1 1110.
1110 in 2's complement is -2, not +14.

questions.q: An 8-bit 2's complement adder adds 10011100 and 01110100. What is the 8-bit result?
questions.explain: 10011100 = -100 and 01110100 = +116. Their binary sum is 1 0001 0000; the carry out is discarded, leaving 00010000 = +16, which is -100 + 116.
why_wrong: Keeps the carry as a ninth bit; the 8-bit register holds only the lower eight bits.
Gives -16, with the wrong sign for the answer.
Adds one extra unit from a mistaken carry.

questions.q: A prototype board has only 2-input NAND gates. What is the minimum number of these gates needed to build a 2-input OR gate?
questions.explain: A + B = NAND(A', B'). Each input inverter is a NAND with tied inputs (2 gates) and the third NAND combines them, so 3 gates in total.
why_wrong: Not enough: two NANDs can only make AND/NOT combinations, not an OR.
This is the minimum for building an XOR gate, not an OR.
More than needed; OR needs just inverters on both inputs and one NAND.

questions.q: A parity unit uses a 4-input XOR (cascaded 2-input XOR gates). For how many of the 16 input combinations is its output 1?
questions.explain: A cascaded XOR outputs 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1. In 4 bits: 4 with one 1 plus 4 with three 1s = 8 combinations.
why_wrong: Counts only the combinations with exactly one 1 input.
Counts only the combinations with exactly two 1 inputs.
Counts every non-zero combination, which is how a 4-input OR behaves.

questions.q: A circuit feeds A and B into a NAND gate and into a NOR gate, then combines both outputs in a final NAND gate. Which single gate does it act like?
questions.explain: Y = NOT[(A.B)' . (A+B)'] = (A.B) + (A+B) = A + B. Truth table: 00 gives 0, and 01, 10, 11 all give 1, which is OR.
why_wrong: XOR would give 0 for A = B = 1, but this circuit gives 1.
NAND would give 1 for A = B = 0, but this circuit gives 0.
XNOR would give 1 for A = B = 0, but this circuit gives 0.

questions.q: A technician applies logic 1 to both inputs of six separate gates: AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR. How many of them give a high output?
questions.explain: With inputs 11: AND = 1, OR = 1, NAND = 0, NOR = 0, XOR = 0, XNOR = 1. So three gates (AND, OR, XNOR) are high.
why_wrong: Misses the XNOR, which gives 1 when both inputs are equal.
Wrongly counts the XOR, which gives 0 when both inputs are equal.
Wrongly counts the NAND and XOR, which both give 0 for inputs 11.

questions.q: A gate acts as an AND gate in positive logic. What function does the same hardware perform in negative logic?
questions.explain: The hardware gives a high output only when both inputs are high. In negative logic high means 0 and low means 1, so the output is logic 1 (low) when at least one input is logic 1 (low). That is OR.
why_wrong: Inverting the logic assignment does not invert the output; it only swaps AND and OR.
NOR would require inverting the output in addition to swapping the logic levels.
The function changes: AND and OR swap when the logic convention is reversed.

questions.q: Which of the following sets of gates is NOT functionally complete (cannot build every Boolean function)?
questions.explain: A set is complete if it can make NOT. AND and OR are both monotone: with inputs all 1 they can only output 1, so they can never produce an inverter.
why_wrong: NAND alone is universal; it can build NOT, AND and OR.
NOR alone is universal; it can build NOT, OR and AND.
With AND and NOT, De Morgan gives OR, so this set is complete.

questions.q: An XNOR gate has one input tied to logic 1 and the other input carries signal A. How does it behave?
questions.explain: XNOR(A, 1) = A.1 + A'.0 = A. With the fixed input at 1 the XNOR passes A unchanged, whereas an XOR with the same tie would invert it.
why_wrong: This describes XOR with one input tied high, not XNOR.
The output depends on A, so it cannot be stuck.
The output depends on A, so it cannot be stuck.

questions.q: A designer's circuit implements Y = A.B + A.B' + A'.B. Which simplified expression gives the same output with the fewest gates?
questions.explain: A.B + A.B' = A(B + B') = A. Then A + A'.B = A + B by the absorption identity X + X'Y = X + Y.
why_wrong: Drops the terms A.B' and A'.B, which are also 1 for some inputs.
This is the NAND function; it differs when A = B = 1.
Fails for A = 0, B = 1 where the original gives 1.

questions.q: A student must simplify Y = (A + B)(A + C) to reduce the gate count. Which is the correct result?
questions.explain: Expanding: (A + B)(A + C) = AA + AC + AB + BC = A + AC + AB + BC = A(1 + C + B) + BC = A + BC. This is the distributive law X + YZ = (X + Y)(X + Z).
why_wrong: Equals A(B + C), which is 0 when A = 0 and B = C = 1 whereas Y is 1.
Treats the product as a sum; Y is 0 when A = 0 and B = 1, C = 0.
Is 0 whenever A = 0, but Y is 1 for A = 0, B = C = 1.

questions.q: A logic designer finds a circuit with Y = A.B + A'.C + B.C. Which expression is the minimal form of Y?
questions.explain: B.C is the consensus of A.B and A'.C. By the consensus theorem XY + X'Z + YZ = XY + X'Z, so B.C can be removed.
why_wrong: Fails for A = 0, B = 0, C = 1 where Y = 1.
Fails for A = 1, B = 1, C = 0 where Y = 1.
Equivalent but not minimal; B.C is redundant (consensus term).

questions.q: A designer must realise Y = NOT(A.B + C) using only inverters, OR and AND gates in the simplest way. Which expression is correct?
questions.explain: By De Morgan, NOT(X + Z) = X'.Z' with X = A.B and Z = C. NOT(A.B) = A' + B', so Y = (A' + B').C'.
why_wrong: Complements AB incorrectly (it should become A' + B') and uses OR instead of AND.
Complements each variable without changing AND/OR properly; the AB term must become A' + B'.
Changes the AND to OR throughout; the outer term should remain a product.

questions.q: A truth table shows Y = 1 for exactly the four rows where C = 1, written as A'B'C + A'BC + AB'C + ABC. What is Y after simplification?
questions.explain: Factor C: C(A'B' + A'B + AB' + AB) = C(A'(B' + B) + A(B' + B)) = C(A' + A) = C.
why_wrong: Only the last of the four terms; Y is 1 for other rows with C = 1.
Is 1 for rows where C = 0 and A = 1, which are not in the list.
Y is 0 for rows where C = 0, so it is not constant.

questions.q: Which of the following Boolean identities is NOT valid?
questions.explain: A.(A + B) = A.A + A.B = A + A.B = A (absorption), not B. For A = 1, B = 0 the left side is 1 but the right side is 0.
why_wrong: This is a valid absorption-type identity.
This is valid: A.A' = 0, leaving A.B.
This is the absorption law and is valid.

questions.q: Simplify (A XOR B) XOR (A XNOR B).
questions.explain: Let X = A XOR B. Then A XNOR B = X', and X XOR X' = X.X + X'.X' = X + X' = 1, so the output is always 1.
why_wrong: A XOR X' is 1, not 0; the two inputs are always opposite.
The result does not depend on A; the inputs are always complementary.
This is just one of the two inner terms, not the combined output.

questions.q: Simplify Y = (A + B).(A' + C).(B + C) to a minimal expression.
questions.explain: (B + C) is the consensus factor of (A + B) and (A' + C) and is redundant. (A + B)(A' + C) = AC + A'B + BC = AC + A'B by the consensus theorem.
why_wrong: Swaps the roles of B and C; fails for A = 1, B = 1, C = 0 where Y = 0.
Fails for A = 1, B = 1, C = 0 where Y = 0.
Too restrictive; Y is also 1 for A = 0, B = 1, C = 0.

questions.q: A 2-input function is specified as F = A + B'. How is F written in canonical SOP form?
questions.explain: F = A(B + B') + B'(A + A') = AB + AB' + A'B' = m3 + m2 + m0. So F = sum of m(0, 2, 3).
why_wrong: This is A + B (OR), not A + B'.
This is A' + B... A'B' + A'B + AB = A' + B, not A + B'.
This is the NAND function A' + B', not A + B'.

questions.q: A 3-input odd-parity detector has F = sum of m(1, 2, 4, 7). Which canonical POS form describes it?
questions.explain: A canonical POS uses the maxterms for rows where F = 0. F = 1 on rows 1, 2, 4, 7, so F = 0 on 0, 3, 5, 6. Therefore F = product of M(0, 3, 5, 6).
why_wrong: Reuses the minterm indices as maxterm indices; maxterms cover the rows where F = 0.
Lists indices that are not the zero rows of F.
Lists indices that mix zero rows and one rows.

questions.q: A comparator circuit has F = (A + B').(A' + B). Which SOP expression is equal to F?
questions.explain: A + B' is 0 only at A = 0, B = 1 and A' + B is 0 only at A = 1, B = 0. So F is 1 at 00 and 11, which is the XNOR: A.B + A'.B'.
why_wrong: This is XOR, the complement of F.
F is 0 for A = 1, B = 0 whereas A + B is 1.
Misses the row A = 0, B = 0 where F = 1.

questions.q: For a 3-variable function A, B, C, which expression is the maxterm M5?
questions.explain: 5 = 101. A maxterm uses the variable complemented when its bit is 1 and un-complemented when 0, joined by OR: A' + B + C'.
why_wrong: Complements the wrong variables; this is M2 (010).
This is the minterm m5, a product rather than the maxterm.
Complements B and C; this is M3 (011).

questions.q: An alarm circuit follows F = A.B + C for three inputs. For how many of the 8 input combinations is F = 1?
questions.explain: A.B is 1 for 110, 111. C is 1 for 001, 011, 101, 111. The union is {001, 011, 101, 110, 111}, with 111 counted once: 5 rows.
why_wrong: Counts only the two rows of A.B plus one row of C.
Counts only the rows where C = 1.
Adds 2 rows of A.B and 4 rows of C without removing the overlap at 111.

questions.q: A function F(A, B, C) is given as the product of M(0, 1, 2). Which is its minimal SOP expression?
questions.explain: F = 0 on rows 0, 1, 2, so F = 1 on 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Rows 4-7 are A; rows 3 and 7 are B.C. Minimal SOP: A + B.C.
why_wrong: This is 1 for m1 and m3 where F = 0 or not at m4.
This is the product M(0) only, which has just one zero.
This is only minterm m7 and misses m3, m4, m5, m6.

questions.q: A 3-variable function is given as the product of M(0, 5). How many minterms appear in its canonical SOP form?
questions.explain: A 3-variable function has 8 rows. Two maxterms (rows 0 and 5) mean F = 0 there, so F = 1 on the remaining 8 - 2 = 6 rows.
why_wrong: These are the zero rows (maxterms), not the minterms.
All 8 rows would be minterms only for the constant function 1.
Halves the table instead of removing the two zero rows.

questions.q: Expand F = A.B + A'.C into canonical SOP over the variables A, B and C. Which minterm list is correct?
why_wrong: Forgets to complement A in the A'.C term (uses A.C instead).
Complements C instead of keeping it, expanding A'.C as A'.C'.
Uses A'.B + A.C, swapping where the complement bar goes.

questions.q: A K-map for F(A,B,C,D) has 1s at minterms 0, 1, 4 and 5 only. What is the minimal SOP?
questions.explain: Minterms 0000, 0001, 0100, 0101 form a 2x2 block in which only B and D vary. A = 0 and C = 0 are constant, so F = A'.C'.
why_wrong: Covers minterms 0, 2, 4, 6, not 0, 1, 4, 5.
Covers minterms 0, 1, 8, 9, not 0, 1, 4, 5.
Covers only minterms 0-3, which includes 2 and 3 where F is 0.

questions.q: A K-map shows 1s at minterms 1, 3, 9 and 11 only. Which is the minimal SOP for F(A,B,C,D)?
questions.explain: 1 = 0001, 3 = 0011, 9 = 1001, 11 = 1011. A and C vary, while B = 0 and D = 1 stay fixed. So F = B'.D.
why_wrong: Covers minterms 5, 7, 13, 15, not 1, 3, 9, 11.
Covers minterms 0, 2, 8, 10, the other column.
Covers minterms 1, 3, 5, 7, which includes 5 and 7 where F is 0.

questions.q: A safety interlock output is 1 at minterms 0, 1, 2, 5, 8, 9 and 10 of (A, B, C, D) and 0 elsewhere. Which is its minimal SOP?
questions.explain: Corners 0, 2, 8, 10 give B'.D'; 0, 1, 8, 9 give B'.C'. Minterm 5 (0101) can only pair with 1 (0001), giving A'.C'.D. Together: B'.D' + B'.C' + A'.C'.D.
why_wrong: Leaves out the 1 at minterm 5 (0101), which neither pair covers.
A'.D also covers 3 and 7, where F is 0.
C'.D also covers minterm 13, where F is 0.

questions.q: A controller output is 1 for minterms 4, 5, 6, 7, 12 and is a don't-care for minterms 13, 14, 15; it is 0 elsewhere. Using the don't-cares, what is the minimal SOP?
questions.explain: Cells 4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15 (the whole B = 1 row-block) form a group of 8 when the don't-cares are used. Only B is constant, so F = B.
why_wrong: Misses minterm 12, which must be covered.
Misses minterms 6 and 7, which must be covered.
Misses minterms 4-7, which must be covered.

questions.q: A 4-variable K-map has 1s at minterms 0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13 and 15. What is the minimal SOP?
questions.explain: Corner cells 0, 2, 8, 10 give B'.D'. The central block 5, 7, 13, 15 gives B.D. So F = B'.D' + B.D, the XNOR of B and D.
why_wrong: This is B XOR D, the complement of F.
Reduces to D', which is 1 on rows where F is 0.
Only two of the four cells in each group are covered; this is not minimal.

questions.q: In a 4-variable K-map, a valid group of 8 adjacent 1s yields a product term with how many literals?
questions.explain: Each doubling of the group removes one variable. 8 cells = 2^3 remove 3 of the 4 variables, leaving a single literal.
why_wrong: Three variables are eliminated, not kept.
This would come from a group of 4 cells.
This would be a single isolated minterm.

questions.q: In a 4-variable K-map, which set of minterms forms a single valid group of 4 (using wrap-around adjacency)?
questions.explain: The four corners 0000, 0010, 1000, 1010 are adjacent by wrap-around in both directions. B = 0 and D = 0 stay constant, giving B'.D'.
why_wrong: These cells are not adjacent in a block; no two variables stay constant.
These cells are scattered; no two variables stay constant.
These cells are scattered; no two variables stay constant.

questions.q: A 4-variable function is given as the product of M(5, 7, 13, 15). Grouping the 0s in the K-map, what is the minimal POS?
questions.explain: Zeros at 0101, 0111, 1101, 1111 have B = 1 and D = 1 constant, so F' = B.D. By De Morgan, F = B' + D'.
why_wrong: Uses un-complemented variables; the zeros have B = 1 and D = 1, so each literal is complemented.
Gives a product instead of a sum; POS terms are OR terms.
Complements only one of the two variables.
